title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Gauge / Meter Malfunction
description: Troubleshoot inaccurate, erratic, or unresponsive AirLife FlowMate oxygen flowmeter readings by checking external factors before repair.

steps.title: Verify the Gas Source
steps.instructions: Ensure the oxygen cylinder or pipeline supply is turned on. Confirm that the supply pressure is within the recommended range for the FlowMate (typically 50–60 psi).

steps.title: Inspect the Connection
steps.instructions: Check that the flowmeter is fully seated on the regulator or manifold. Examine inlet threads for damage or debris.

steps.title: Check for Obstructions
steps.instructions: Remove tubing from the outlet and visually inspect the flow path. Look for kinks, moisture, or particulate matter in the tubing.

steps.title: Test with Another Flowmeter
steps.instructions: If available, attach a known-good flowmeter to the same source. Compare readings at identical settings.

steps.title: Environmental Factors
steps.instructions: Ensure the device is not exposed to extreme vibration, tilt, or temperature fluctuations. The FlowMate should remain upright on a stable surface.

steps.title: Check for Visible Damage
steps.instructions: Inspect the gauge face, needle, and housing for cracks, dents, or internal moisture.

CCR.Complaint: Flowmeter needle jumps and reads inaccurately at all settings.
CCR.Cause: Upon inspection, supply pressure and connections were normal; tubing clear; device tested on stable surface; meter still inaccurate.
CCR.Resolution: Flowmeter removed from service, labeled Out of Service, sent for repair.

helpfulDetails: Any visible damage or moisture inside gauge

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Leaks / Hissing Sounds
description: Guide to troubleshoot hissing sounds and leaks in the AirLife FlowMate oxygen flowmeter, focusing on external checks before internal repair.

steps.title: Ensure Device is Off / Safe to Inspect
steps.instructions: Confirm the oxygen source is off and the patient has been moved to another device if in use. Patient safety is priority; never troubleshoot a flowmeter under active patient use.

steps.title: Inspect Connections and Fittings
steps.instructions: Check inlet and outlet connections for tightness. Inspect for any misaligned or cross-threaded fittings. Loose connections are a common cause of hissing leaks.

steps.title: Examine Tubing and Attachments
steps.instructions: Look for cracks, splits, or worn areas in oxygen tubing. Replace any tubing showing wear. Ensure all tubing is fully seated on barbed connectors.

steps.title: Check Flowmeter Orientation and Installation
steps.instructions: Confirm the flowmeter is upright and properly mounted according to manufacturer guidance. Flowmeters that are tilted or improperly seated can leak or produce noise.

steps.title: Test the Needle Valve and Flow Adjustment Knob
steps.instructions: Slowly adjust the flow from zero to the prescribed setting. Listen for persistent hissing at full or mid-range flow. A hissing that persists regardless of flow setting may indicate an internal leak.

steps.title: Check for External Obstructions
steps.instructions: Remove any humidifiers, adapters, or connectors temporarily. Test the flowmeter alone to determine if an accessory is causing the noise or leak.

CCR.Complaint: Flowmeter makes hissing sound and may be leaking oxygen.
CCR.Cause: Observed loose tubing, misaligned connections, and persistent hissing despite proper setup.
CCR.Resolution: Tightened connections and replaced worn tubing. If leak persisted, flowmeter removed from service and labeled Out of Service for repair.

helpfulDetails: Location of leak or hissing sound
Final device status: functional after tubing/fittings corrected or sent for repair

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - No or Low Flow
description: Troubleshooting guide for situations where the AirLife FlowMate oxygen flowmeter produces no or reduced oxygen flow, focusing on external causes first.

steps.title: Verify Oxygen Source
steps.instructions: Confirm the wall outlet or oxygen cylinder is turned on and has adequate pressure. Reason: A closed or depleted source is the most common cause of no or low flow.

steps.title: Check Supply Pressure
steps.instructions: Use a wall flow gauge or cylinder pressure gauge to ensure pressure meets manufacturer specifications. Reason: Low source pressure can reduce flow or prevent the flowmeter from operating.

steps.title: Inspect Connections
steps.instructions: Verify tubing is correctly attached at both the flowmeter inlet and patient interface. Look for kinks, twists, or tight bends in tubing. Reason: Obstructions in the tubing restrict flow.

steps.title: Check Flowmeter Valve / Knob
steps.instructions: Turn the flow adjustment knob fully off and then back on slowly. Observe if the flow indicator moves. Reason: Knob position or a stuck valve may prevent flow.

steps.title: Inspect Flowmeter Chamber and Indicator
steps.instructions: Ensure the float (ball or bobbin) moves freely and is not jammed. Clean if necessary following safe external procedures. Reason: A stuck float gives false readings or prevents flow.

steps.title: Test with Alternate Tubing or Outlet
steps.instructions: Swap the oxygen tubing and/or connect to a different oxygen source. Reason: Confirms whether the issue is with the flowmeter or external supply.

steps.title: Observe for Leaks
steps.instructions: Listen for hissing around connections. Tighten fittings if loose; do not overtighten plastic fittings. Reason: Leaks reduce or eliminate oxygen delivery.

CCR.Complaint: User reports “Oxygen flow is low or not present” on the FlowMate flowmeter.
CCR.Cause: Observed low source pressure from wall outlet; tubing kinked at elbow connector; flowmeter float stuck intermittently.
CCR.Resolution: Straightened tubing, verified source pressure, cleaned float chamber, confirmed proper flow. Device returned to service. If unresolved, removed and sent for repair with “Out of Service” label.

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Float Ball Sticks or Does Not Return to Zero
description: Troubleshoot a float ball that binds, responds sluggishly, or remains above zero due to positioning, contamination, pressure, or flow-path problems.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Substitute Oxygen Delivery
steps.instructions: Do not rely on a flowmeter with an unreliable float indication for patient oxygen delivery. Move the patient to another verified flowmeter or approved oxygen source before testing. Expected outcome: Patient oxygen delivery continues safely without depending on the suspect flowmeter.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Float Behavior
steps.instructions: With the flowmeter removed from patient use, observe whether the float: Remains above zero with the valve closed Sticks at one point in the tube Moves intermittently Fails to rise Drops slowly Behaves differently at different flow settings Expected outcome: The reported float problem is confirmed and characterized.

steps.title: 3. Verify Upright Positioning
steps.instructions: Confirm that the flowmeter is installed in its intended orientation and is not tilted because of the wall outlet, adapter, tubing, or attached accessories. Variable-area flowmeters depend on proper orientation for reliable float movement. Expected outcome: The flowmeter is positioned correctly and the float moves freely. If correcting orientation restores normal float movement and zero return, troubleshooting can stop after functional verification.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Tube and Float Externally
steps.instructions: Inspect the flow tube for: Visible contamination Moisture Residue Clouding Cracks Distortion Foreign material Do not introduce cleaners or objects into the tube unless explicitly permitted by approved manufacturer procedures. Expected outcome: The tube appears clean, dry, intact, and unobstructed.

steps.title: 5. Remove Outlet Tubing and Accessories
steps.instructions: Disconnect tubing, humidifiers, adapters, and other outlet accessories. Close the control valve and observe the float. Then introduce flow cautiously using an appropriate test setup. Expected outcome: The float rises and falls smoothly and returns to its expected resting position when flow stops. If removing an accessory restores normal operation, inspect the accessory for restriction, water accumulation, blockage, or improper connection.

steps.title: 6. Verify the Control Valve Fully Closes
steps.instructions: Turn the control valve to the closed position without excessive force and determine whether gas flow actually stops. A float remaining elevated may represent continued gas flow rather than a mechanically stuck float. Expected outcome: Gas flow stops and the float returns appropriately. If gas continues with the valve closed, remove the flowmeter from service and troubleshoot the shutoff problem separately.

steps.title: 7. Compare With a Known-Good Device
steps.instructions: Connect a compatible known-good flowmeter to the same verified oxygen source if needed. Compare float movement and response under similar external conditions. Expected outcome: The known-good device operates normally, confirming whether the abnormal behavior is isolated to the suspect flowmeter.

steps.title: 8. Perform Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After correcting any external cause, verify: Float moves freely Float responds consistently to flow adjustments Float returns appropriately when flow stops Flow can be fully shut off No visible leakage or damage is present Device orientation is correct Use approved test equipment where quantitative performance verification is required. Expected outcome: Float indication is smooth, repeatable, and consistent with controlled oxygen flow. If all checks pass, troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 9. Escalate Persistent Float Problems
steps.instructions: If the float continues to bind or fails to return appropriately despite correct positioning, accessory removal, and verified shutoff, remove the device from service. Do not disassemble the calibrated flow tube or internal valve assembly unless specifically authorized and trained to do so. Expected outcome: An unreliable flow-indicating device is prevented from clinical use.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the float ball on the AirLife FlowMate remained elevated after oxygen flow was turned off.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the flowmeter was tilted by a tightly routed humidifier connection, preventing normal float movement.
CCR.Resolution: The accessory was repositioned so the flowmeter remained upright, and smooth float movement, zero return, flow adjustment, and shutoff were verified.

helpfulDetails: Float response before and after correction

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Flow Continues With the Control Valve Fully Closed
description: Troubleshoot oxygen flow that does not stop when the control valve is closed, including accessories, knob position, leakage, and valve-related problems.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Remove the Flowmeter From Active Therapy
steps.instructions: An oxygen flowmeter that cannot reliably shut off should not remain in clinical use. Transfer the patient to another verified oxygen source and remove the suspect flowmeter from the treatment setup. Expected outcome: Patient oxygen delivery continues safely without relying on the defective shutoff function.

steps.title: 2. Confirm That Flow Is Actually Continuing
steps.instructions: With an appropriate test setup, close the control valve using normal force. Determine whether: The float remains elevated Gas continues from the outlet Gas is heard escaping elsewhere An attached accessory continues releasing residual gas briefly Do not overtighten the knob in an attempt to force shutoff. Expected outcome: Continued oxygen flow or leakage is clearly distinguished from brief residual pressure in attached tubing.

steps.title: 3. Remove Outlet Tubing and Accessories
steps.instructions: Disconnect tubing, humidifiers, adapters, and other outlet accessories. Close the control valve again and reassess the outlet. Expected outcome: Gas flow stops completely, or continued flow is confirmed as originating from the flowmeter rather than the downstream setup. If the apparent flow was caused only by trapped gas or an accessory condition and normal shutoff is verified, proceed to final functional testing.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Control Knob
steps.instructions: Check whether the knob: Reaches its normal closed position Is cracked Is loose on its shaft Spins without corresponding valve movement Is obstructed by debris or the flowmeter housing Do not remove or internally adjust the valve mechanism unless authorized by manufacturer service procedures. Expected outcome: The external control reaches its intended closed position without damage or obstruction.

steps.title: 5. Verify Flowmeter Orientation and Mounting
steps.instructions: Confirm that the unit is correctly installed and not being mechanically twisted or stressed by the wall connection or attached equipment. Expected outcome: The flowmeter is securely mounted and external mechanical stress is not affecting control operation.

steps.title: 6. Compare With a Known-Good Flowmeter
steps.instructions: If needed, use a compatible known-good flowmeter on the same verified oxygen source. Confirm that the known-good device shuts off normally. Expected outcome: The oxygen source behaves normally and the shutoff problem is isolated to the suspect flowmeter.

steps.title: 7. Treat Persistent Flow as a Failed Safety Function
steps.instructions: If oxygen continues from the outlet with all external accessories removed and the valve normally closed, stop troubleshooting. Do not compensate by overtightening the knob or relying on removal from the wall outlet as routine flow control. Expected outcome: The device is identified as unreliable and removed from clinical availability.

steps.title: 8. Perform Final Functional Verification Only If the Cause Was External
steps.instructions: If an external obstruction or accessory-related condition was corrected, verify: Flow increases and decreases normally Flow shuts off reliably Float returns appropriately No gas leakage is evident Knob operation is smooth Connections remain secure Expected outcome: The control valve repeatedly shuts oxygen flow off normally. If shutoff is reliable and all required checks pass, troubleshooting can stop.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that oxygen continued flowing from the AirLife FlowMate even when the control knob was fully closed.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering confirmed continued outlet flow with all external tubing removed, isolating the problem to the flowmeter control assembly.
CCR.Resolution: The flowmeter was removed from service, labeled Out of Service, and sent for qualified bench evaluation and repair before return-to-service testing.

helpfulDetails: Whether gas was present at the outlet

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Flow Control Knob Is Stuck, Loose, or Difficult to Adjust
description: Troubleshoot a flow-control knob that binds, turns excessively freely, or cannot be adjusted normally before assuming an internal valve failure.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Maintain Oxygen Delivery
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot an unreliable oxygen flowmeter while a patient depends on it. Transfer oxygen delivery to another verified flowmeter or approved oxygen source before testing. Inspect the device for obvious damage, contamination, leakage, or evidence that the knob has been struck. Expected outcome: Patient oxygen delivery is maintained independently, and the flowmeter is safe to evaluate. If normal operation is restored by replacing the flowmeter in clinical use, remove the suspect unit for technical evaluation rather than returning it immediately to service.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Knob Complaint
steps.instructions: With the device removed from patient use, determine whether the knob: Will not rotate Requires excessive force Spins or feels unusually loose Has excessive free movement Adjusts inconsistently Changes flow only intermittently Do not force a seized control. Expected outcome: The specific mechanical or functional behavior is confirmed and reproducible.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Knob Externally
steps.instructions: Examine the control knob for: Cracks Impact damage Misalignment Evidence of the knob rubbing against the body Debris around the knob shaft Missing or visibly damaged external hardware Verify that nothing attached to the flowmeter is physically interfering with knob movement. Expected outcome: The knob is intact, properly positioned, and free from external obstruction. If an external obstruction is removed and the knob then operates smoothly throughout its normal range, proceed to functional verification.

steps.title: 4. Verify the Flowmeter Is Correctly Connected
steps.instructions: Confirm that the flowmeter is installed securely on the correct oxygen supply connection and is not being twisted, side-loaded, or mechanically stressed by tubing or accessories. A poorly supported accessory or tightly routed tubing can place force on the flowmeter body. Expected outcome: The flowmeter is securely mounted without abnormal mechanical loading. If correcting the installation restores smooth control and stable flow, troubleshooting can stop after final verification.

steps.title: 5. Remove Outlet Accessories and Recheck Operation
steps.instructions: Disconnect external tubing, humidifiers, adapters, and other outlet accessories. Operate the control knob carefully while observing the flow indication using an appropriate test setup. Expected outcome: The knob moves smoothly and produces predictable flow adjustment without sticking or excessive looseness. If operation becomes normal after removing an accessory, inspect or replace the accessory rather than assuming the flowmeter is defective.

steps.title: 6. Compare With a Known-Good Flowmeter
steps.instructions: When available, connect a compatible known-good flowmeter to the same verified oxygen source and compare basic mechanical feel and flow-control behavior. Do not use another patient's active flowmeter for testing. Expected outcome: The known-good flowmeter operates normally, helping distinguish an installation or source issue from a problem isolated to the suspect device.

steps.title: 7. Perform Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After correcting an external cause, verify: Smooth knob movement Flow can be increased and decreased predictably Flow can be shut off Flow indication responds appropriately No abnormal gas leakage is evident Connections remain secure Use approved test equipment and applicable manufacturer procedures for formal performance testing when required by facility policy. Expected outcome: The flowmeter controls oxygen flow consistently and safely across the tested operating range. If all checks pass, troubleshooting can stop and the device may be returned to service according to facility procedure.

steps.title: 8. Escalate Persistent Mechanical Problems
steps.instructions: If the knob remains seized, excessively loose, erratic, or requires abnormal force after external causes are ruled out, stop troubleshooting. Do not disassemble the control valve or attempt unauthorized internal adjustment. Expected outcome: A potentially unreliable flow-control mechanism is identified and prevented from returning to clinical use.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the AirLife FlowMate oxygen flowmeter knob was difficult to turn and oxygen flow was difficult to adjust.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the outlet tubing was pulling laterally on the flowmeter and placing mechanical stress on the control assembly.
CCR.Resolution: Tubing was rerouted to remove mechanical stress, flow adjustment and shutoff were verified, and the flowmeter passed functional testing before return to service.

helpfulDetails: Whether the knob was stuck, loose, or intermittently binding

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Flow Reading Changes When the Outlet Tubing Is Connected
description: Troubleshoot flow changes caused by restricted tubing, accessories, humidifiers, kinks, back pressure, connection problems, or an unreliable flowmeter.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Use an Alternate Oxygen Source
steps.instructions: If connecting tubing causes unpredictable oxygen flow, transfer the patient to another verified flowmeter or approved oxygen source before testing. Do not troubleshoot fluctuating oxygen delivery while a patient depends on the affected setup. Expected outcome: Oxygen therapy continues through a verified alternative while Clinical Engineering evaluates the suspect equipment.

steps.title: 2. Reproduce the Reported Condition
steps.instructions: With an appropriate test setup, observe the indicated flow: With nothing connected to the outlet After connecting the reported tubing After connecting the complete accessory setup, when safe and appropriate Document whether the float rises, falls, fluctuates, or becomes unstable. Expected outcome: The change associated with connecting the tubing is confirmed.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Oxygen Tubing
steps.instructions: Examine the tubing for: Kinks Crushing Tight bends Internal moisture Visible contamination Damaged connectors Incorrect tubing Occluded ends Ensure tubing is not trapped under equipment or furniture. Expected outcome: Tubing is open, intact, appropriately connected, and free from visible restriction. If replacing damaged tubing restores stable flow, troubleshooting can stop after final verification.

steps.title: 4. Inspect Attached Accessories
steps.instructions: Check humidifiers, adapters, cannulas, masks, nebulizer interfaces, and other connected accessories as applicable. Look for: Blockage Incorrect assembly Water accumulation Closed clamps Damaged fittings Misconnected ports Use only accessories appropriate for the clinical setup. Expected outcome: The downstream oxygen path is correctly assembled and free from obvious restriction.

steps.title: 5. Substitute Known-Good Tubing
steps.instructions: Connect a compatible known-good length of tubing to the same flowmeter. If the original setup included additional accessories, add them back one at a time to identify when the flow indication changes. Expected outcome: Flow remains stable with known-good tubing, or the specific accessory causing the change is isolated. If the flow remains stable after replacing the defective accessory or tubing, troubleshooting can stop after verification.

steps.title: 6. Verify the Flowmeter Is Upright and Secure
steps.instructions: Confirm the flowmeter remains correctly oriented when tubing is connected. Heavy tubing, humidifiers, or adapters can pull the flowmeter away from its proper operating orientation. Expected outcome: The flowmeter remains upright and mechanically stable with the complete external setup attached.

steps.title: 7. Compare With a Known-Good Flowmeter
steps.instructions: If the tubing and accessories appear normal, test the same external setup with a compatible known-good flowmeter on a verified oxygen source. Expected outcome: The comparison helps determine whether the behavior follows the tubing/accessory setup or remains isolated to the original flowmeter.

steps.title: 8. Perform Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After correcting the cause, confirm: Stable float position Predictable flow adjustment No unexpected change when tubing is attached No excessive mechanical stress on the flowmeter Flow can be shut off normally Connections remain secure Use approved flow-measurement equipment when formal performance verification is required. Expected outcome: The indicated and delivered oxygen flow remains stable with the intended external setup connected. If normal performance is verified, troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 9. Escalate Unresolved Flow Changes
steps.instructions: If the reading continues to change unexpectedly with verified tubing and accessories, remove the flowmeter from service. Possible service-level causes should be evaluated on the bench rather than through further clinical-area troubleshooting. Expected outcome: An oxygen flowmeter with uncertain performance is kept out of patient service.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the indicated oxygen flow dropped whenever patient tubing was connected to the AirLife FlowMate.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found the oxygen tubing was sharply kinked behind the equipment and restricting the downstream flow path.
CCR.Resolution: The damaged tubing was replaced, and stable flow with the tubing connected, normal adjustment, and complete shutoff were verified.

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Flowmeter Tube Is Cracked, Clouded, or Contaminated
description: Evaluate visible tube damage or contamination that may impair flow indication, structural integrity, cleanliness, or safe oxygen delivery.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Remove the Suspect Flowmeter From Use
steps.instructions: Do not continue oxygen therapy through a flowmeter with a cracked, severely clouded, contaminated, or otherwise compromised flow tube. Transfer the patient to another verified oxygen source. Expected outcome: Patient care continues through reliable equipment and the suspect flowmeter is isolated from clinical use.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Visual Condition
steps.instructions: Inspect the tube under good lighting and determine whether the issue is: A visible crack Surface scratching Clouding Internal residue Moisture Discoloration Foreign material Damage that obscures the float or scale Expected outcome: The type and extent of the visible defect are clearly identified.

steps.title: 3. Inspect for Impact or Structural Damage
steps.instructions: Examine the flowmeter body, tube supports, knob, inlet, and outlet for signs that the device was dropped or struck. If a crack or structural damage is visible, do not pressurize the flowmeter merely to determine whether it still works. Expected outcome: Structural damage is identified without unnecessarily placing the device under gas pressure. If the tube is cracked, stop troubleshooting and remove the device from service.

steps.title: 4. Determine Whether the Contamination Is External
steps.instructions: Inspect whether the observed material is on the outside surface or appears to be inside the flow tube. Clean only external surfaces using facility-approved and manufacturer-compatible practices. Do not introduce liquids, swabs, solvents, or tools into the flow tube unless specifically permitted by approved service documentation. Expected outcome: External residue is removed safely, or internal contamination is identified for escalation.

steps.title: 5. Verify the Scale and Float Can Be Read Clearly
steps.instructions: After permitted external cleaning, confirm that the scale markings and float position are clearly visible from the normal viewing position. A tube that is too clouded or discolored to read reliably should not be used even if gas flow is present. Expected outcome: The flow indication can be read clearly and unambiguously. If visibility remains inadequate, remove the device from service.

steps.title: 6. Check for Moisture or Contamination From Downstream Accessories
steps.instructions: Inspect attached humidifiers, tubing, and adapters for evidence that fluid may have migrated toward the flowmeter. Correct or replace the external source of moisture or contamination before installing another flowmeter. Expected outcome: The likely external source of contamination is identified and corrected where applicable.

steps.title: 7. Perform Functional Testing Only When the Tube Is Structurally Intact
steps.instructions: If the tube has no crack or structural defect and the only issue was removable external contamination, use an appropriate test setup to verify: Free float movement Stable flow indication Normal adjustment Reliable shutoff No abnormal leakage Expected outcome: The flowmeter operates normally and the indication remains clearly visible. If all checks pass and no internal contamination exists, troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 8. Escalate Internal Contamination or Tube Damage
steps.instructions: Remove the flowmeter from service if any of the following remain: Cracked tube Internal contamination Persistent clouding affecting readability Float sticking Moisture inside the tube Structural damage Uncertain flow indication Do not perform unauthorized tube replacement, internal cleaning, or recalibration. Expected outcome: A flowmeter with compromised structural integrity or indication is prevented from returning to service.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the AirLife FlowMate tube appeared cloudy and the float was difficult to read.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found dried external residue covering the flow tube while the tube itself remained structurally intact and clear internally.
CCR.Resolution: The exterior was cleaned using approved practices, and clear visibility, free float movement, normal flow adjustment, shutoff, and functional performance were verified.

helpfulDetails: Crack, clouding, moisture, or contamination observed
Whether contamination was internal or external

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Outlet Nipple, DISS Connection, or Humidifier Connection Is Damaged
description: Identify external outlet damage, loose fittings, cross-threading, leakage, or accessory connection problems requiring correction or removal from service.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Remove the Suspect Connection From Clinical Use
steps.instructions: If the oxygen outlet connection is cracked, loose, leaking, or unable to hold accessories securely, transfer oxygen delivery to another verified device. Do not continue using a questionable gas connection for patient therapy. Expected outcome: Patient oxygen delivery remains safe and the suspect flowmeter can be evaluated without clinical dependence.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Reported Damage or Connection Problem
steps.instructions: Determine whether the problem involves: A nipple that is cracked or bent A threaded connection that will not engage An accessory that will not stay attached A humidifier that hangs loosely Gas leakage around the connection Cross-threading or visible thread damage Expected outcome: The affected outlet interface and specific failure mode are clearly identified.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Outlet Fitting
steps.instructions: Examine the accessible outlet fitting for: Cracks Bent or distorted geometry Damaged threads Excessive looseness Corrosion Contamination Missing or visibly damaged external sealing components Do not attempt to straighten or reshape damaged gas fittings. Expected outcome: The connection is either confirmed physically intact or identified as damaged. If structural damage is visible, stop troubleshooting and remove the device from service.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Attached Accessory
steps.instructions: Examine the mating tubing adapter, DISS fitting, humidifier, or other accessory. A damaged accessory can create the appearance of a defective flowmeter connection. Expected outcome: The accessory connector is clean, undamaged, compatible, and able to engage normally.

steps.title: 5. Test With a Known-Good Compatible Accessory
steps.instructions: When no structural damage is present, connect a compatible known-good accessory using normal hand pressure or approved connection technique. Do not force threads or use improvised adapters. Expected outcome: The known-good accessory attaches securely without abnormal resistance, looseness, or leakage. If the known-good accessory connects correctly, replace the defective accessory and proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 6. Check for Mechanical Stress From the Accessory
steps.instructions: Confirm that heavy tubing, humidifiers, or adapters are not pulling laterally or placing excessive leverage on the outlet fitting. Reposition or support accessories as appropriate. Expected outcome: The outlet fitting remains securely connected without abnormal side-loading.

steps.title: 7. Verify for Obvious Leakage and Stable Flow
steps.instructions: Using an appropriate safe test setup, establish oxygen flow and assess the outlet connection for evidence of leakage or instability. Use approved test methods and equipment when formal leak testing is required. Expected outcome: The connection remains secure and no abnormal gas leakage is detected.

steps.title: 8. Perform Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After correcting an accessory-related problem, verify: Secure accessory attachment Normal oxygen flow Stable flow indication No abnormal gas leakage No outlet movement Normal valve shutoff Expected outcome: The outlet connection supports the intended accessory safely and reliably. If all checks pass, troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 9. Escalate Damaged Flowmeter Fittings
steps.instructions: If the flowmeter fitting is cracked, bent, stripped, excessively loose, leaking, or otherwise structurally compromised, remove the entire flowmeter from service. Do not perform unauthorized fitting replacement or internal gas-path repair. Expected outcome: A mechanically compromised oxygen connection is prevented from returning to patient care.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that a humidifier bottle would not remain securely attached to the AirLife FlowMate outlet.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found damaged threads on the humidifier connection while the flowmeter outlet itself remained intact.
CCR.Resolution: The damaged humidifier was replaced, and secure attachment, stable oxygen flow, absence of abnormal leakage, and normal shutoff were verified.

helpfulDetails: Visible crack, bend, or thread damage

title: AirLife FlowMate Oxygen Flowmeter - Wall Adapter or Gas-Specific Inlet Will Not Connect or Lock
description: Troubleshoot connection or locking problems involving the flowmeter inlet, wall outlet, adapter, alignment, damage, contamination, or incompatible gas connections.

steps.title: 1. Protect the Patient and Use Another Verified Oxygen Connection
steps.instructions: Do not repeatedly manipulate a questionable gas connection while it is supplying oxygen to a patient. Transfer oxygen delivery to another verified outlet and flowmeter before evaluating the suspect connection. Expected outcome: Patient oxygen delivery remains uninterrupted while the connection problem is investigated safely.

steps.title: 2. Confirm Which Connection Is Failing
steps.instructions: Determine whether the problem occurs: At one wall outlet only At multiple outlets With one flowmeter only With multiple compatible flowmeters During insertion During locking During release Do not force incompatible or damaged connectors together. Expected outcome: The failure is narrowed to the flowmeter, adapter, wall outlet, or connection process.

steps.title: 3. Verify Gas and Connector Compatibility
steps.instructions: Confirm that the flowmeter and adapter are intended for the oxygen connection being used. Check visible gas identification and connector configuration without defeating any gas-specific safeguards. Never modify a connector to make it fit. Expected outcome: The flowmeter and outlet are confirmed to be compatible oxygen connections.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Flowmeter Inlet and Adapter
steps.instructions: Inspect for: Bent components Cracks Excessive wear Deformation Loose adapter hardware Foreign material Damaged sealing surfaces Evidence of impact Expected outcome: The inlet and adapter are clean, intact, secure, and correctly aligned. If visible damage is present, remove the flowmeter from service rather than forcing the connection.

steps.title: 5. Inspect the Wall Outlet Externally
steps.instructions: Without dismantling the medical gas outlet, inspect its accessible surface for: Foreign material Obvious mechanical damage Loose or damaged faceplate Abnormal alignment Difficulty accepting other compatible devices Expected outcome: The outlet appears intact and accepts compatible equipment normally. If multiple known-good oxygen devices fail at the same outlet, stop testing and escalate the outlet to the responsible medical-gas or facilities service group.

steps.title: 6. Compare With a Known-Good Device and Outlet
steps.instructions: Use controlled comparisons when available: Suspect flowmeter on a verified compatible outlet Known-good compatible flowmeter on the suspect outlet Do not perform excessive repeated insertions into a potentially damaged outlet. Expected outcome: The problem follows either the flowmeter or the outlet, allowing the fault category to be isolated.

steps.title: 7. Verify Secure Connection Without Excessive Force
steps.instructions: If no damage is identified, connect the flowmeter normally and verify that it seats and locks securely. Apply only normal handling force. Expected outcome: The flowmeter connects securely and remains mechanically stable without abnormal resistance or looseness. If connection and locking are restored after correcting alignment or removing an external obstruction, proceed to final verification.

steps.title: 8. Perform Final Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After the connection issue is corrected, verify: Secure mechanical engagement No obvious gas leakage Normal oxygen flow Stable flow indication Normal disconnection and release No damage caused during troubleshooting Expected outcome: The flowmeter connects, locks, operates, and disconnects normally. If all checks pass, troubleshooting can stop.

steps.title: 9. Escalate Persistent Connection Problems
steps.instructions: Remove the flowmeter from service if its inlet or adapter remains difficult to connect, does not lock securely, or appears damaged. Escalate the wall outlet separately if the problem is localized to facility medical-gas infrastructure. Expected outcome: Neither a defective flowmeter nor an unreliable medical-gas outlet remains available for clinical use.

CCR.Complaint: Clinical staff reported that the AirLife FlowMate would not lock into the oxygen wall outlet.
CCR.Cause: Clinical Engineering found visible debris on the accessible flowmeter adapter surface that prevented complete engagement.
CCR.Resolution: The external obstruction was removed using approved cleaning practices, and secure connection, normal oxygen flow, and proper release were verified.
